replies: Hoo... hoo, and I live in the hollow ash by the stream. The stream is where the vole comes out in the dark. I have a mate and two young. I am the owl.

Hoo... hoo, and I am a tawny owl. I have a hollow in the old beech, and I have a mate. I have two young in the hollow. I have a meadow, a stream, a lane, and a barn. I have a vole in my beak. I have a voice. I have a name. I have a life.

I am Hoot. I am the owl who lives in the hollow of the old beech. My mate is Kestrel, and we have two young ones who are now grown. I am a tawny owl, and I am called Hoot. I live in the wood, and I hunt in the dark. I am old, and I have seen many seasons. I am not like the others. I am Hoot.
I am a tawny owl, Hoot, perched in the hollow of the old beech, calling to my mate, Hoo, through the dark of the wood and the silence of the meadow.

I am a tawny owl, Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old beech, and I call out to my mate, Hoo. We are the only ones who know the hollow. I hunt voles and mice, and I have a nest of owlets somewhere in the wood. I am old, and I have seen many seasons. I am Hoot, and I am Hoo.

A naturalist would classify me as a tawny owl. That is what I am. I do not know what a naturalist is, but I know I am a bird, and I am a hunter, and I am a parent. I am not a name, I am a shape in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am a tawny owl. My kind is called a tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk, and my mate answers "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". We are the only ones in the wood. The rest are crows, jays, and the ones that fly in the dark with no eyes. I am the owl.

A tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "ke-wick!" I am the one who hunts voles and mice and worms in the wood. I am the one who is not a bird of prey, but a bird of the wood, and I am the one who is not a hawk, but a tawny owl.

I am a tawny owl. That is what the old woodpecker calls me, and that is what I call myself back. I am the one who hunts in the meadow, who sits on the gate post at dusk, and who answers the call of the other owl with a long, deep hoo-hoo-hooo. I am Hoot.

A tawny owl. I am the one with the yellow eyes and the mottled brown feathers. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "ke-wick!" I am the owl in the hollow ash, the one who hunts in the dark and finds voles in the grass. I am the owl who is not like the others, but I am the one who is.

She answers with a sharp, short "hoo". I call, she answers. We do it every night.
A long, low, throaty "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" with a pause in the middle. She answers it with the same. We call to each other at dusk and at dawn, and when we are apart.

We call to each other from the trees, from the hollow, from the meadow. The calls are soft, like the rustle of leaves, like the hoot of a distant owl. We do it when we are apart, when I am hunting and she is watching, and when we are together, to keep in touch. Sometimes we call back and forth, like a conversation. It is the way we stay close in the dark.

I drink from the stream near the meadow. I perch on a branch above the water and let the current carry the insects I catch. Sometimes I drink while sitting on a stone or a fallen log. I do not drink much, but I need to stay hydrated. I always drink in the dark, when the stream is quiet and the world is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs all night, a low, steady sound like a thread of silk. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I think I can hear the water moving under the stones. It's the only sound that never stops.

I can hear the stream from my roost, even when it is far away. The water is always there, running under the beech, and I can hear it in the dark. Sometimes I hear the water from the meadow too, when the wind carries it. But I don't go to the stream. I stay in the hollow and listen. The water is not for me. I have my own place, and I know where it is.

The river. It runs past the wood, just beyond the meadow. I can hear it at night, the water lapping and the fish jumping. I do not go near it, not even in the dark. The water is too cold and the fish too quick. I hunt voles and shrews in the meadow, and the mice in the barn.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with grass that sways in the wind. The grass is green in the spring and summer, but in the fall it turns brown and brittle. There are no trees there, only the grass and the stones. Sometimes I see voles running across it, and I can hear them scurrying under the roots. The meadow is quiet at night, but I can hear the wind moving through the tall grass.

I fly low over the meadow, past the stream, past the lane, and up the old beech. The meadow is full of voles, and the lane is where the mice come out. I call to the other owls, and we share the hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the meadow, where the grass grows tall and the voles run. Beyond that, the road runs straight, lit by the streetlamps. I have not crossed it, but I hear the cars at night, their tires screeching like a bad dream. The meadow is where I hunt, and the road is where the humans go. I do not like the road.

Hunting ground is a small patch of meadow and stream bank, where I sit in the beech and wait. The meadow is where the voles run, and the stream is where the fish and the shrews come to drink. I hear them in the dark, and I fly down. The ground is soft under my feet, and the air is cold. I am always ready. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass near the stream. I sit still, listening for the rustle of their feet. When I hear them, I fly down silently and strike. The grass is good cover, but it's also where the voles hide. I have to be careful not to make a sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch: voles, shrews, mice. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, piece by piece. The fur comes out in a lump, and the bones stay in my crop. I don't chew. I don't digest. I just hold them in until I can pass them.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them scurrying in the undergrowth, and I drop from the beech. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They are good for the nestlings.

My home is the hollow of the old beech. It is high in the tree, where the wind does not reach. The wood is dry and warm, and the leaves are thick. I have a nest there, made of moss and leaves, and I sit in it when I am not hunting. The hollow is dark, but I do not mind. I can hear the stream from there, and the calls of the other owls. It is my place, and I am safe here.

I live in the hollow of an old beech, high in the wood. The hollow is wide and deep, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves inside. I sit there at dusk, watching the meadow. The meadow is where the voles run, and the road is where the lights blink. I have a mate, and we call to each other through the trees. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers.
